Son of Zeus and the strongest of the Greek heroes. To atone for killing his family in a madness sent by Hera, he served King Eurystheus and completed twelve labors, from the Nemean Lion to bringing Cerberus up from the underworld.

The great hero of Ulster. As a boy he killed the smith Culann's fierce hound and offered to guard in its place, earning the name 'Hound of Culann'; in the Cattle Raid of Cooley he held the fords of Ulster alone.
The old, wise singer of the Kalevala, whose songs could shape the world. He sang the boastful young Joukahainen into a swamp, and led the voyage to win the Sampo back from Pohjola.
A warrior of the Genpei War in the late 1100s. The Tale of the Heike calls her a fearless rider and archer, a match for any warrior, who fought beside Kiso Yoshinaka in his last battle.

The legendary king of Britain. In Malory the Lady of the Lake gives him Excalibur, and Merlin tells him its scabbard is worth ten of the sword, for whoever wears it loses no blood. He fell at Camlann fighting Mordred.

A huntress of Arcadia, raised in the wild, who joined the hunt for the Calydonian boar. She would marry only a man who could outrun her; Hippomenes won by dropping three golden apples that she stopped to pick up.

King of Ithaca, famed for cunning. He devised the wooden horse that ended the Trojan War, wandered ten years on the way home, and returned disguised as a beggar to string his great bow and reclaim his house.
The greatest Greek warrior at Troy, son of King Peleus and the sea-nymph Thetis. A later tradition says his mother dipped him in the river Styx, leaving only the heel she held unprotected.
Greek goddess of fortune and chance, shown with a rudder, a wheel, or a horn of plenty. Cities honored her as the keeper of their luck.

A Gaulish god known mostly from carvings: antlered, often holding a torc, among animals. His name survives on the Pillar of the Boatmen in Paris, and an antlered figure on the Gundestrup cauldron is often identified with him.
Norse god of thunder, son of Odin, who defends gods and people against the giants with his hammer Mjölnir, which returns to his hand.

A giantess and goddess of winter, skiing, and the hunt. When the gods killed her father Thjazi she came to Asgard seeking amends; Loki made her laugh, and she chose a husband, Njord, by his feet alone.
The lioness goddess of war and healing. Ra sent her as his Eye to punish humankind, then stopped her rampage by flooding the fields with beer dyed red, which she drank as blood.
Greek god of the sea, earthquakes, and horses, brother of Zeus, who wields the trident. When King Laomedon of Troy cheated him he sent a sea monster against the city, which Heracles slew.
The Egyptian sun god, who sails the sky in his boat by day and the underworld by night, where the serpent Apep tries to swallow him before each dawn.
An Irish goddess of battle and fate who appears as a crow. In the Táin she offers Cú Chulainn her love; when he refuses, she hinders him in his fights.
In Greek myth the shades are the spirits of the dead, pale shadows that drift through the underworld; in the Odyssey they crowd around Odysseus' offering to drink its blood.

Storm-winged 'snatchers' who, in the tale of the Argonauts, fouled the food of the blind seer Phineus until the winged sons of the North Wind drove them away.

Wild spirits of the woods and hills who follow Dionysus, part human and part goat or horse, known for revelry and mischief.
Sea creatures whose song lured sailors to their deaths. Odysseus stopped his crew's ears with wax and had himself tied to the mast to hear them safely.
In the Norse sagas the draugr is the walking dead: a corpse that rises from its burial mound, unnaturally strong and heavy, to guard its treasure or haunt the living.
Sparks from Muspelheim, the burning realm of the south. At the world's beginning its sparks met the ice of Niflheim; at Ragnarök its sons ride out with Surtr.
Half bull and half man, born to Pasiphaë, queen of Crete, and kept by King Minos in the Labyrinth that Daedalus built, until Theseus killed it with Ariadne's help.
One-eyed giants. Hesiod's Cyclopes forged the thunderbolts of Zeus, while in the Odyssey the shepherd Polyphemus trapped Odysseus' men in his cave until Odysseus blinded him.
The Gorgons were three sisters with snakes for hair whose gaze turned onlookers to stone. Of the three, only Medusa was mortal.
The mortal Gorgon, whose gaze turned onlookers to stone. Perseus beheaded her while watching her reflection in his polished shield.
The greatest Greek warrior at Troy. A later tradition says his mother dipped him in the river Styx, leaving only his heel unprotected.
The youngest Titan, who overthrew his father Ouranos with a sickle and swallowed his own children to keep his throne, until Zeus forced him to give them back.

In the Ironwood east of Midgard an old giantess bore a brood of giants in wolf shape; among such wolves are Sköll and Hati, who hunt the sun and moon across the sky.
The monstrous wolf, a son of Loki. The gods bound him with the magic fetter Gleipnir, and Tyr lost his hand in the wolf's jaws; at Ragnarök Fenrir breaks free and swallows Odin.
The trickster of the Norse gods, a shape-shifter who helps and harms them by turns. After the death of Baldr he is bound beneath a serpent's dripping venom until Ragnarök.
The fire giant who guards Muspelheim with a flaming sword. At Ragnarök he leads the sons of Muspell against the gods and his fire engulfs the world.

The scarab beetle, rolling its ball of dung, was a sacred image of Khepri, the god who rolls the rising sun across the sky; scarab amulets were placed over the hearts of the dead.

Egyptians preserved the bodies of the dead so the soul could return to them. Their stories also tell of the restless dead, like the ghost who complains to the priest Khonsuemheb that his tomb has crumbled.
Small figures buried with the dead, inscribed with a spell that called them to do the owner's work in the afterlife: 'Here I am,' the shabti answers.
The desert's snakes were a real danger, and the Book of the Dead holds spells to drive back serpents that threaten the dead on their journey.
The Devourer of the Dead, part crocodile, part lion, part hippopotamus. She waits beside the scales where a person's heart is weighed against the feather of Maat, and eats the hearts that fail.
God of storms, the desert, and disorder, who murdered his brother Osiris and fought Horus for the throne. Yet he also stands at the prow of Ra's boat and spears the serpent Apep.
The great serpent of chaos who attacks the sun god's boat each night in the underworld. Priests recited spells to overthrow him so the sun would rise again.

A warrior woman of Alba who trained heroes in arms on her island fortress. Cú Chulainn learned his feats from her, and she gave him the spear Gáe Bolg.

The Fomorian king whose one eye destroyed whatever it looked upon; it took several men to lift its lid. His grandson Lugh struck the eye with a sling-stone at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired.

Man-eating birds of the marsh of Stymphalus, driven off by Heracles as one of his labours. Pausanias says they were the size of cranes, like ibises but with stronger, straight beaks.
The birds of Stymphalus shed their feathers like arrows: Apollonius tells how one wounded an Argonaut as they sailed past the island of Ares, and how the heroes drove them off with clashing shields.

The hound of Hades, who guards the gate of the underworld: he fawns on those who enter and devours any who try to leave. Apollodorus gives him three dogs' heads, a serpent for a tail, and snakes' heads along his back. Bringing him up from below was the last of Heracles' twelve labours.

Death, son of Night and brother of Sleep, with a heart of iron. In Euripides' Alcestis he comes for the queen who gave her life for her husband, and Heracles wrestles him by her tomb and brings her back.

The last child of Earth and Tartarus, who rose against the gods: from his shoulders grew a hundred snakes' heads with fiery eyes, and below his thighs were huge coils of vipers. Zeus struck him down with thunderbolts and buried him under Mount Etna.

Demeter's daughter, carried off by Hades to be queen of the dead. Because she ate a pomegranate seed below, she spends part of every year in the underworld; when she returns, the earth blooms again and it is spring (Homeric Hymn to Demeter).

The singer of Thrace, son of a Muse, whose song moved beasts, trees and stones. He sailed with the Argonauts and drowned out the Sirens with his lyre; when his wife Eurydice died, he sang his way down to the dead and moved even Hades and Persephone to let her go, but he looked back too soon and lost her.

The bergrisar, the mountain giants of the north. Snorri tells how one of them, in disguise as a builder, offered to wall Asgard in a single winter, with his stallion Svadilfari hauling the stones, and was paid instead with Thor's hammer.

The strongest of the giants, whose heart was of hard stone, sharp-pointed with three corners, and whose head too was stone. He fought Thor with a stone shield and a whetstone; Thor's hammer shattered the whetstone and then his skull.

Lord of the giants, who stole Thor's hammer and hid it eight leagues under the earth, asking Freyja as his bride for its return. Thor came in her place, in a bridal veil, and took the hammer back at the wedding feast.

The first of all beings, formed from the rime where the ice of Niflheim met the heat of Muspell, the father of the frost giants. Odin and his brothers slew him and made the world from his body: the earth from his flesh, the sea from his blood, the sky from his skull.

The All-Father, who gave an eye for a drink from Mimir's well of wisdom and hung nine nights on the windswept tree, a sacrifice of himself to himself, to win the runes. His ravens Huginn and Muninn fly over the world each day and bring him news; his spear Gungnir never misses.

Goddess of love and of the slain: half of those who fall in battle go to her hall, Folkvangr. She owns the necklace Brisingamen and a cloak of falcon feathers that lets the wearer fly, which she lent to Loki to find Thor's stolen hammer.

The Geat who came over the sea to the hall of Heorot and fought the monster Grendel bare-handed, tearing off his arm with the grip of thirty men. He went down into the mere after Grendel's mother and killed her with an ancient sword made by giants, and in old age died killing a dragon.

In Malory's tales of Arthur, knights in black armour hold the fords and the fields against all comers, and every knight-errant must ride through them.
Hunting hounds run through the Welsh tales: Pwyll first meets the king of the Otherworld when their hounds cross on the hunt.
A lake monster of Welsh tradition, so heavy and strong that it took oxen to drag it from its lake; the old Triads tell of the flood that broke out when it burst its lake.
The wandering light over bogs and marshes in British folklore, which leads travellers who follow it astray into the mire.
In Culhwch and Olwen, Twrch Trwyth runs with his seven young pigs, Grugyn Silver-bristle and Llwydawg the Hewer among them, and Arthur's men must hunt them all.

A giant knight, green from head to foot on a green horse, who rode into Arthur's hall at Christmas and offered a beheading game. Gawain struck off his head, and he picked it up by the hair and rode away, to return the blow a year later.
Arthur's son and betrayer, who seized the kingdom while Arthur was abroad. At the last battle at Camlann, father and son struck each other down.

A king turned into a monstrous boar for his wickedness. Arthur and his men hunted him across Ireland and Wales to win the comb, the razor and the shears between his ears, which Culhwch needed to win Olwen.

She rode past the mound of Arberth on a pale-white horse, and no rider could catch her however hard they chased, until Pwyll called out and asked her to stop. Her birds sing so sweetly that the dead wake and the living fall asleep.

King of Annwn, the Otherworld, first met hunting with his hounds, shining white with red ears. He and Pwyll traded places and faces for a year, and Pwyll fought his enemy for him.

Scorpion-people guard the gate of Mount Mashu, where the sun goes in and out; their terror is awesome and their glance is death. They let Gilgamesh pass on his search for Utnapishtim. Tiamat made scorpion-men among her eleven monsters.
The 'big weather-beast', a lion-headed demon with a man's body and bird's feet. Tiamat made the ugallu among her eleven monsters; later the Assyrians carved them at their doors to keep evil out.
The umu dabrutu, 'raging storms', are among the eleven monsters Tiamat made to fight the gods in the Enuma Elish: whirling storm-beasts that tear across the land.
In the Enuma Elish, Tiamat gives birth to monster serpents, sharp of tooth, their bodies filled with venom instead of blood.

The guardian Enlil set over the Cedar Forest, whose roar is the flood and whose breath is death, wrapped in seven radiances of terror. Gilgamesh and Enkidu went to the forest to fight him, and Shamash sent thirteen winds to hold him fast.

When Gilgamesh spurned Ishtar, she made her father Anu give her the Bull of Heaven. At its snort the earth split open and men fell into the pits, until Enkidu seized it by the horns and Gilgamesh struck it down.

The salt sea, mother of all. In the Enuma Elish she makes eleven monsters, storm-demons, scorpion-men and serpents, to fight the young gods, until Marduk splits her in two and makes heaven and earth from her body.

Hiisi is the demon of the wild woods and rocky hills of Finnish tradition. In the Kalevala it was Hiisi who made the great elk that Lemminkäinen had to hunt down on skis.
Pohjola, the dark land of the North, has wolves and bears at its mistress's call. When Kullervo took his revenge, he drove wolves and bears home in place of the cattle.
To win the Maid of the North, Ilmarinen had to plough Pohjola's field of vipers, writhing with snakes, with a plough of gold and silver.
Pakkanen, the Frost, son of the North wind, was sent by Louhi to freeze Lemminkäinen's ship fast in the sea, until Lemminkäinen sang him back with words of his origin.

In the first of Rostam's Seven Labours, a lion came upon him while he slept in a reed bed, and his horse Rakhsh fought and killed it alone.

A water-maiden of rivers and pools in Slavic folklore, pale, with long loose hair, who sits on the bank combing it and draws the unwary into the water.

In the tale of Tsarevich Ivan and the Firebird, a great grey wolf eats Ivan's horse, then carries him on its back and helps him win the Firebird, the horse with the golden mane and Elena the Beautiful.
The Firebird of the Russian tales, whose feathers shine like flame and light up a whole dark room; it came at night to steal the tsar's golden apples.
The great dragon of the old Russian heroic songs, the byliny, with many heads, who carried off a prince's niece; the hero Dobrynya Nikitich fought him at the river and freed his captives.
The bony-legged old witch of the Russian forest, who flies in a mortar, steers with a pestle and sweeps away her tracks with a broom. Her hut stands on hen's legs and turns round at a word.

Paracelsus wrote that the undines are the spirits of water, living in it as we live in air, and that they look most like human beings of all the elemental folk.
The sea-fairies of Breton folklore, with long golden hair, who sing on the rocks and draw sailors down to their shining palaces beneath the waves.
When the sea gates were opened, the great city of Ys was drowned in a night. Breton songs say its bells can still be heard ringing under the sea off the bay of Douarnenez.
King Gradlon's black horse, whose name means "sea-horse". It could gallop over the waves, and on it the old king escaped as the sea swallowed Ys.
The servant of death in Breton tradition: a tall, gaunt figure with a wide hat and a scythe whose blade turns outward. Whoever hears the creaking axle of his cart at night knows someone will die.

King Gradlon's daughter. She stole the golden key of the sea gates from her sleeping father and opened them, and the sea drowned the city of Ys. The tales say she lives on beneath the waves as a mari-morgan.
Dahut takes the shape of a mari-morgan!
The sea is a road, and I run on it.
Do you hear the axle creak? It creaks for you.
The key was so small, and the sea so big. Let it in.
Lord of the sea, my city is already yours.
Paracelsus wrote that the sylphs are the spirits of the air, swifter and lighter than men, living in the air as we live on the earth.
In Aristophanes' comedy The Birds, the birds of every kind, owls, jays, crows and many more, gather to build a city in the sky and cut the gods off from mankind.
Cloud-Cuckoo-Land was built in the air between earth and heaven, where the smoke of men's offerings had to pass on its way up to the gods.
Once King Tereus of Thrace, turned into a hoopoe, he is king of the birds in Aristophanes' comedy. He calls the birds together to hear the plan for their city in the clouds.
The swift messenger of the gods, on golden wings. In The Birds she flies straight into the birds' new city on an errand from Zeus and is caught at the walls.
The giant bird of the Thousand and One Nights, so vast it hid the sun and fed its young on elephants. When Sindbad's shipmates broke its egg, the Rocs dropped boulders on their ship.
Come, all you birds! Here is one who walks on the ground.
I carry the gods' word, and I do not stop for walls.
You broke the egg. Now look up.
Another wanderer far from home. Stay, and be a bird with us.
Defeat Gífr and Geri before they change their watch a third time. An ember aura.
They sleep by turns so that none may pass; pass before the turns run out.
Defeat Víðófnir with a Fire hit as the final blow. Adds the Lævateinn Shard passive.
Only one weapon can fell the gleaming cock, and it is made of fire.
Defeat Garmr before he bays a third time. A crown of rime aura.
Silence the hound before the cave hears him thrice.
Defeat Níðhöggr with a Holy hit as the final blow. Adds the Dew of the Ash passive.
What gnaws in the dark at the roots of the world fears the light.
Defeat Morvarc'h without it ever hurting you. A sea-foam aura.
The old king rode out of the flood untouched; ride out of this one the same.
Defeat Dahut with a Lightning hit as the final blow. Adds the Golden Key passive.
The sea opened the city; let the storm close the story.
Defeat Iris within 60 s of her coming. A rainbow aura.
The birds caught the swift messenger at their walls; be quicker than her errand.
Defeat the Roc without a single boulder landing on you. Adds the Roc's Feather passive.
Watch the shadows on the ground, and let every stone miss.
God meters fill 5% faster per level.
The Realm of the Ten Suns
Bands of scorching heat cross the land!
In Journey to the West, the White Bone Demon is a spirit of white bones who tries to trick the pilgrims so she can eat the monk Tang Sanzang and live forever.
The ancient Classic of Mountains and Seas tells of a fox with nine tails in the hills of Qingqiu. In later tales fox spirits are clever shape-shifters with foxfire at their command.
When all ten suns rose together, the Huainanzi says, the crops burned and the plants withered, and monsters and fierce beasts came out to prey on the people.
The beast of Chinese New Year folklore that came down at the turn of the year. It feared loud noise, fire and the colour red, which is why firecrackers are set off and red is hung on doors.
The White Bone Demon of Journey to the West. Three times she came to the pilgrims in disguise, as a village girl, an old woman and an old man, and three times the Monkey King saw through her.

Once ten suns crossed the sky by turns, but in the time of the sage-king Yao they all rose together and scorched the earth. The archer Yi shot down nine, and in each that fell was a crow; one sun was left to light the world.
Her true shape shows: strike now!
Ten suns blaze! Shoot down nine, and leave one in the sky.
The great archer of ancient China. When ten suns rose together and burned the world, he shot down nine of them with his arrows, and he slew the monsters that plagued the land.
A fan of two long-range arrows that pierce.
Every 6 s he looses a great arrow at the strongest boss or flying monster in range (else the toughest monster): double damage against bosses and flyers.
The 10:00 boss of the Realm of the Ten Suns.
The 20:00 boss of the Realm of the Ten Suns.
The 30:00 boss of the Realm of the Ten Suns.
Lend me your strength, and my arrows will not miss.
The year turns, and I come down from the mountain.
Only a poor traveller, nothing to fear. Come closer.
Ten of us, all at once. Let the world burn.
The archer again. Nine of us remember your arrows.
One sun in the sky is enough, Ra; we are ten.
The chaos at the heart of the Unweaving: where the myths fray, it pulls their threads apart. It fights with what it has stolen from the monsters you have beaten, and it unravels the gods themselves.
The 30:00 boss of the Crossroads, the finale.
Defeat the 30:00 boss in %d levels (%d so far).
Every story ends. I am how.
Twelve labours, and still one more. I will unpick them all.
Little sun. The serpent only swallowed you; I will unweave you.
Frighten Nian 5 times with Fire or Lightning before you defeat it. A red-lantern aura.
The villagers drove the beast off with noise, fire and red; give it all three, again and again.
Shoot down the nine suns within 120 s of their rising. Adds the Sun-crow Feather passive.
A crow lived in every sun; when Yi's arrows struck, nine fell from the sky one after another.
Defeat the Unweaver before it unweaves your gods a fourth time. Adds the Loose Thread passive.
Cut the last thread before it pulls the rest loose.
Defeat the Unweaver without it ever unweaving a full god meter of yours. A many-coloured thread aura.
What is spent can't be stolen: call your gods before the threads come.
The Keres were the dark spirits of violent death. On the battlefield, the Shield of Heracles says, they fought over the fallen, dark, with gnashing teeth and blood-stained cloaks.
In 1127, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says, many men saw and heard huntsmen in the woods by night; the huntsmen were black and loathsome, and their hounds were all black and wide-eyed and ugly.
A spectre of Hecate's who haunts lonely roads. In The Frogs she appears on the way to the underworld: now a bull, now a mule, now a lovely woman, now a dog, her face aflame and one leg of bronze.

A daemon of the underworld, painted by Polygnotus at Delphi. He eats the flesh of the dead and leaves only their bones; his colour is blue-black, like the flies that settle on meat, he shows his teeth, and he sits on a vulture's skin.

A host of the dead that rides through the night sky. In 1127 men at Peterborough saw it: big black huntsmen on black horses and black goats, with black, wide-eyed hounds, and heard their horns all night long.
Bull or dog or woman? Look again; I've changed.
Fresh dead. I'll leave you the bones.
Hear the horns? The Hunt is riding, and you are the quarry.
Mistress Hecate! Your hound of the roads has found someone.
A pale mist settles; you feel a strange languor...

In 1746 the scholar-monk Augustin Calmet gathered the reports from Hungary, Moravia and Serbia of the dead who left their graves at night to trouble the living, and were found in their coffins fresh and ruddy.
Small black bats that come out of the ruins at dusk. The vampire stories of the 1800s are full of them, flitting at the windows of the sleepers.
Small black bats that come out of the ruins at dusk, sweeping across in long flights.

Sir Francis Varney, the vampire of a long penny serial. Tall and gaunt, his face white, his teeth like fangs. Again and again he is shot or struck down, and again and again the cold rays of the moon bring him back to life.

A nobleman of London society with a dead grey eye and a deathly pale face. In Polidori's tale he travels with young Aubrey, dies in Greece, swears him to silence for a year and a day, and returns to prey on Aubrey's sister.

Mircalla, Countess Karnstein, dead for more than a hundred years. As the lovely, languid guest Carmilla she visits Laura's Styrian castle; by night she comes as a sooty-black creature like a monstrous cat, and her victims slowly waste away.
Carmilla becomes a monstrous black cat!
Strike me down if you like. The moon is up.
Remember your oath: speak of me to no one.
Don't be afraid, darling. You will be mine, and I yours.
Queen of the dead? I have slept in my tomb a hundred years; it never kept me.
The full moon rises over the forest!

Gerald of Wales heard in Ireland of the people of Ossory, two of whom, a man and a woman, had to put off their human shape every seven years and live in the forests as wolves. A priest met one by night, and it spoke to him like a man.
Black ravens wheel over the forest, following the wolves to whatever they bring down.

A Breton baron who became a wolf in the forest three days of every week. His wife learned his secret and had his clothes hidden, so he could never turn back, until the king, who loved the gentle wolf, had them given back to him.
Bisclavret has his clothes: he is a man again!

A knight of Arthur's court with a ring of two stones: touched with the white, he became a wolf; with the red, a man again. In Ireland his wife took the ring and left him a wolf, and he gathered a pack of wolves and ravaged the land until Arthur came.

From 1764 to 1767 a beast terrorised the mountains of the Gévaudan in France. Witnesses said it was as big as a calf, reddish, with a black stripe down its back, a broad chest and great teeth, and that it sprang on its victims from the undergrowth.
Grr... Find what was hidden from me, and I'll be a man again.
The white stone made me a wolf. Now I lead the pack.
(A low growl from the undergrowth. Something huge is watching.)
My king! You came all the way to Ireland for me?
Walpurgis Night: the witches ride over the mountain!

On Walpurgis Night, the eve of May Day, German folklore says the witches ride up the Brocken in the Harz on broomsticks, pitchforks and goats. Johannes Praetorius gathered the tales in 1668; Goethe sent Faust up among them.
The goats the witches ride up the mountain on Walpurgis Night, shaggy and black, butting through the heather.

Climbers on the Brocken sometimes saw a giant figure in the mist below them, surrounded by a ring of rainbow light, that moved when they moved. In 1780 Johann Silberschlag described it: it was their own shadow, cast on the cloud.
In Goethe's Walpurgis Night the witches' chorus sings as they climb the Brocken: old Baubo comes alone, riding on a farrow sow, and the whole crowd follows after her.

A hag of Leicestershire folklore with a blue face and long iron claws. She dug a cave in the Dane Hills with her claws, Black Annis' Bower, and crouched there under an oak to spring out on whoever came by.
(A giant shape in the mist moves when you move.)
Make way! Old Baubo rides alone, and the whole crowd after her!
I dug my bower with these claws. I'll dig you out of yours.
A queen of witches? On my hill there's only one.
Defeat Eurynomos before he devours 10 monsters. A bone-white aura.
He grows fat on the fallen; give him nothing to eat.
Defeat the Wild Hunt before it rides 8 times. Adds the Hunter's Horn passive.
The horns blew all night long at Peterborough; end the hunt before dawn.
Defeat Varney without letting him rise again: stand over him while he lies in the moonlight. A moonlight aura.
The moon gives him back his life. Stand between them.
Defeat Carmilla without her bite ever landing on you. Adds the Pedlar's Charm passive.
The pedlar sold charms against the oupire; be charmed, and never bitten.
Give Bisclavret back his clothes twice before you defeat him. A wolf-grey aura.
The king was kind to the gentle wolf; be kind more than once.
Defeat the Beast of Gévaudan without a single pounce landing on you. Adds the Wolf's Tooth passive.
Watch where the undergrowth stirs, and never be there.
Defeat the Brocken Spectre within 60 s of its coming. A glory of rainbow light.
It is only your own shadow; walk straight through the mist to meet it.
Defeat Black Annis before she goes back to her bower a third time. Adds the Iron Claw passive.
She hides in her bower to mend. Don't give her the time.
Molten metal spills from the forges!

The Völuspá names the dwarves the gods shaped from the blood of Brimir and the bones of Bláinn; in the rocks and under the earth they became the finest smiths in the worlds, makers of the gods' treasures.
A broad dwarf in mail carrying a great forge hammer, guarding the halls where the treasures of the gods were made.

The boar with golden bristles that the dwarf Sindri forged in the fire while his brother Brokkr worked the bellows, and that they gave to Freyr. It runs over the sky and the sea faster than any horse, and its bristles shine so that the darkest night is as bright as day.

The dwarf who wagered his head with Loki that his brother Sindri could forge better treasures than the sons of Ívaldi. While he worked the bellows a fly stung him again and again; at the last sting he paused, and Mjölnir came out short in the handle.
Brokkr works the bellows! Sting him before the treasure is made!
The hammer is forged! Brokkr strikes harder!

A dwarf who lived as a pike in the waterfall Andvarafors and guarded a hoard of gold. When he was caught and robbed of it, down to the little ring Andvaranaut, he laid a curse on the ring: it would be the death of whoever owned it.
Andvari's ring lies there. Take it, and take its curse.
(The golden boar's bristles light the hall like day.)
Keep back! A wager's a wager, and I'm at the bellows.
Take the gold, then. Take the ring. It will be the death of you.
Thor! How's the handle on that hammer? A little short, I'd say.
The light fails in the deep places...
Snorri tells of two kinds of elves: the light elves, fairer than the sun, and the dark elves, who live down in the earth and are blacker than pitch, unlike them in every way.

The warriors of the land of the Nibelungs, who guarded the great hoard in a hollow mountain. Siegfried overcame them, and their twelve giants, and their dwarf lord Alberich, and made the hoard his own.

"All-wise", a pale-nosed dwarf who lived under stone and came to claim Thor's daughter as his bride. Thor asked him the names of all things in every world, and he answered every one, until the sun rose and its light turned him to stone.

Two dwarf brothers who killed the wise Kvasir and let his blood run into two vats, Són and Boðn, and a kettle, Óðrerir. Mixed with honey it became the mead that makes whoever drinks it a poet or a scholar.
Fjalar and Galar brew their mead! Tip the vats!

The strong dwarf who guarded the Nibelung hoard. He owned the Tarnkappe, a cloak that made its wearer invisible and gave him the strength of twelve men, until Siegfried wrestled it from him and made him keeper of the hoard in his own name.
Ask me anything. I know the names of all things in every world.
A drink? It's very good mead. Kvasir is in it.
You can't see me, but I see you.
Thor! Ask your questions, then. The night is long.
Clouds of spores drift through the city!
The mushroom-folk of Mycendra, squat and slow, shuffling out of the gloom under their broad spotted caps. (Mythriven's own creature.)
Small puffballs that drift through the air of Mycendra in clouds, trailing spores. (Mythriven's own creature.)
Flies lit a pale green by the fungus light they feed on, darting across the city in long streams. (Mythriven's own creature.)
A puffball as big as an ox, its skin split and leaking. Every blow that lands makes it burst in a cloud of spores. (Mythriven's own creature.)
The great web of fungus threads that holds Mycendra together, heaving itself up from the ground. Wherever it passes, its threads stay. (Mythriven's own creature.)
The oldest and tallest mushroom of Mycendra, with a face in its stalk. Wherever its spores fall, new mushrooms swell and burst. (Mythriven's own creature.)
(It wheezes. Spores puff from its cracks with every breath.)
(The ground itself heaves, pale threads reaching for your feet.)
Grow, my children. Grow, and burst.
Spring goddess, everything that rots comes back to me.
The hive's tunnels are giving way!

When plague emptied Aegina, King Aeacus prayed to Zeus beneath an oak full of ants and asked for as many subjects. That night the ants became men, the Myrmidons: thrifty, hard-working and tireless, as ants are.

In the desert of India, Herodotus says, live ants smaller than dogs but bigger than foxes, which throw up gold-bearing sand as they dig their burrows; they are swift and fierce, and chase whoever steals the gold.
Ants of the hive on their swarming flight, streaming over the sand in long lines.
A worker ant carrying a lump of gold sand back to its queen. Kill it before it gets there.

The greatest of the gold-digging ants of India. The Indians came for the gold sand it threw up at the hottest hour, on their swiftest camels, and fled at once, because the ants smelled them and gave chase, faster than any other creature.
The ant smells the thief! Run!

An Attic girl, a favourite of Athena. When the goddess invented the plough, Myrmex told everyone it was her own idea, and Athena turned her into an ant, which ever since has gathered the grain the plough sows.
The Queen of the Gold-Digging Ants
The Queen of the Gold-Digging Ants
The mother of the gold-digging ants, vast and winged, lying at the heart of the hive. All the gold her workers dig up is carried to her.
The 10:00 boss of The Myrmidon Hive.
The 20:00 boss of The Myrmidon Hive.
Defeat The Queen of the Gold-Digging Ants
The 30:00 boss of The Myrmidon Hive.
(It lifts its head from the sand. It can smell gold on you.)
The plough was my idea! Well... it should have been.
Bring me the gold, my children. All of it.
Daughter of the grain-mother! Every seed the plough sows, we ants gather.
Spoil Brokkr's forging three times before you defeat him. Adds the Draupnir passive.
A fly stung the smith again and again; be the fly.
Defeat Andvari without anyone taking his cursed ring. A pike-scale aura.
Every owner of that ring came to grief. Leave it where it lies.
Turn Alvíss to stone three times before you defeat him. A dawn-light aura.
Keep him talking; the sun is coming up.
Tear Alberich's cloak off him twice before you defeat him. Adds the Tarnkappe Thread passive.
Siegfried wrestled the cloak from the dwarf; feel for him in the dark.
Defeat the Great Puffball without breathing its spores. A spore-cloud aura.
Every blow makes it burst. Strike and step back.
Stamp out ten of the Spore Mother's mushrooms before you defeat her. Adds the Glow-cap passive.
Take three heaps of the Gold-Digging Ant's gold before you defeat it. A gold-dust aura.
The Indians came for the gold on their swiftest camels. Be swift.
Defeat the Queen of the Gold-Digging Ants before three carriers reach her. Adds the Ant's Strength passive.
Her workers bring her gold. Let none arrive.
Elf-shot! Unseen arrows fly from the trees!
There is a place called Álfheimr, Snorri says, where the people called light elves live; they are fairer to look upon than the sun.
In the old ballads the elf-knight rides out of the greenwood blowing his horn, and whoever hears it is drawn after him.
The Erlking's daughters, who dance in the night mist by the willows. "My daughters shall wait on you," the Erlking promises the child, "and rock you and dance you and sing you to sleep."

On the night before his wedding Sir Oluf rode out and found the elves dancing. The Erlking's daughter held out her hand and asked him to dance; he would not, and she struck him over the heart, and he was dead by morning.
"Dance with me!" Stay in the ring until the dance ends!
The great smith the poem calls prince of elves. King Níðuðr lamed him and set him on an island to forge for him; Völundr took his revenge, forged himself wings, and rose laughing into the air.

The king of the elves who comes to a child riding through the wind and the night in his father's arms. He promises games and flowers and his daughters' dancing; and if the child is not willing, he will use force.
The Erlking beckons... you're drawn toward him!
Welcome! Come, step into the ring and dance with me.
They lamed me so I could not run. So I made wings.
And if you're not willing, I'll use force.
Lady of the Vanir, your brother's realm is mine tonight.
An elfin glamour falls over everything...
At Halloween, Tam Lin tells Janet, the fairy folk will ride: first the black steeds, then the brown, and then the milk-white, with bells ringing on their bridles.

A young knight stolen by the Queen of the Fairies. On Halloween Janet pulled him from his milk-white steed and held him while they turned him in her arms into an adder, a bear, a lion and a burning iron. She held on, and won him back.
You held him fast! Tam Lin is free for a moment!

An elf-knight whose horn drew Lady Isabel from her bed to follow him. He meant to drown her as he had drowned seven king's daughters before her, but she lulled him to sleep with his head in her lap, and killed him with his own dagger.
The Elf-Knight blows his horn... you follow the sound!

The queen who met Thomas under the Eildon Tree, in grass-green silk, fifty silver bells and nine on her horse's mane. She took him to Elfland for seven years, and warned him not to touch the fruit of her garden.
You ate the fruit of Elfland: your tongue is bound, your gods fall silent!
Hold me fast and fear me not. I'll do you no harm.
Hear my horn? Come away with me to the greenwood.
I'm but the queen of fair Elfland, come here to visit you.
Lady of the otherworld! Your horse is slow; mine has fifty silver bells.
A herd stampedes across the hills!
When Pholus opened the centaurs' common jar of wine for Heracles, the other centaurs smelled it and came running to the cave, armed with rocks and pine trees.
Birds beyond counting nested in the woods by the Stymphalian lake in Arcadia, until Heracles scared them up with a bronze rattle and shot them down.
A hind with golden horns, sacred to Artemis. Eurystheus ordered Heracles to bring it back alive, and he chased it for a whole year before he caught it, wearied, at the river Ladon.
A huge boar that ravaged the land from Mount Erymanthus. Heracles chased it out of a thicket with shouts, drove it, worn out, into the deep snow, and caught it in a snare.
The boar is stuck fast in the snow!

The savage king of Arcadia, who served human flesh at his table to test whether his guest was truly Zeus. Zeus brought his house down with a thunderbolt; Lycaon fled into the silent fields and, howling, became a wolf.
Lycaon howls... and becomes a wolf!
(A flash of gold antlers between the trees, and it's gone again.)
(It snorts steam into the cold air and lowers its tusks.)
Sit, guest, and eat. You won't ask what the meat is.
(The hind looks at you. It remembers a whole year of running.)
The swamp rises, thick and foul!
On Athena's advice Cadmus sowed the teeth of the dragon he had killed, and armed men sprang up out of the earth: the Spartoi, the sown men.
While Heracles fought the Hydra, Hera sent a huge crab out of the marsh to help it, and it bit his foot. He killed it; Hera set it among the stars as the Crab.

One of the sown men who sprang from the dragon's teeth. When Cadmus threw a stone among them they turned on one another, each thinking another had thrown it, until only five were left. Echion was one of the five.
You throw the stone among the sown men: they turn on each other!

The water-serpent of the Lerna marsh, child of Typhon and Echidna, with nine heads, the middle one immortal. For every head Heracles cut off, two grew back, until Iolaus seared the necks with burning brands; the immortal head Heracles buried under a heavy rock.
The last head is immortal! Bury it under the rock!
(It raises both claws and scuttles sideways, never turning its back.)
I rose from a dragon's tooth, and I'm still standing. Who threw that stone?
(The heads remember the club and the torches. They hiss louder.)
Dance three of the Erlking's Daughter's dances to the end without ever stepping out, then defeat her. An elf-light aura.
Sir Oluf would not dance, and died of it. Dance.
Defeat the Erlking before he lures anyone a fourth time. Adds the Elf-arrow passive.
The father rode hard through the night. Ride harder.
Free Tam Lin three times by holding on through his changes, then defeat him. A milk-white aura.
Hold him fast and fear him not, whatever shape he takes.
Defeat the Queen of Elfame without anyone eating the fruit of Elfland. Adds the Rhymer's Tongue passive.
Thomas was warned not to touch the fruit. Heed the warning.
Defeat the Ceryneian Hind before it bounds away ten times. A golden-horn aura.
Heracles needed a whole year. You don't have one.
Let Zeus' thunderbolts strike Lycaon three times, then defeat him. Adds the Thunderstone passive.
Keep the host where the god's anger falls.
Throw the stone among Echion's sown men three times, then defeat him. A sown-bronze aura.
Cadmus didn't fight the sown men. He let them fight each other.
Sear five of the Hydra's necks with Fire, then defeat it. Adds Iolaus' Brand passive.
Every head you cut grows two. Every head you burn stays gone.
God meters fill 5% faster per level.
Statuses you cause last 6% longer per level.
The warriors of Ghorvast, broad and grey-skinned, in crude leather and iron. (Mythriven's own creature; the old word "orc" comes from Old English orcneas and Latin Orcus.)
Orcs of Ghorvast who shoot from the walls with crude bows. (Mythriven's own creature.)
The biggest orcs of Ghorvast, swinging great axes. (Mythriven's own creature.)
Carrion crows wheeling in black clouds over the walls of Ghorvast.
A huge orc with a great war drum slung before him. Every beat calls more of Ghorvast to the fight. (Mythriven's own creature.)
The undefeated champion of Ghorvast's fighting pit, scarred all over. Every blow he takes only makes him angrier. (Mythriven's own creature.)
The master of Ghorvast in black iron, horned and terrible. Where his war banner flies, his warriors will not break. (Mythriven's own creature.)
The Warlord plants his banner! Tear it down!
(BOOM. BOOM. BOOM. The whole stronghold answers the drum.)
Hit me. Go on. Hit me harder.
Under my banner, no one runs.
A war god? Good. Mine is a war without gods.
The halls twist, and the light fails...
The soldiers of King Minos, who guarded the palace and the young Athenians sent as tribute to the Minotaur.
Lean young bulls of the Cretan herds, of the line of Poseidon's white bull.

The white bull Poseidon sent up from the sea for Minos to sacrifice. Minos kept it and sacrificed another; Poseidon made it savage, and it ravaged Crete until Heracles caught it and carried it to Greece.
King of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa, who kept the Minotaur in the Labyrinth and fed it Athenian youths. Odysseus saw him in the underworld with a golden sceptre, giving judgement to the dead.
Minos condemns you! Come before him for judgement!

Asterion, the son of Pasiphaë, with a bull's face on a man's body, shut by Minos in the Labyrinth Daedalus built. Theseus found him by the light of Ariadne's thread and killed him with his bare fists.
(It paws the paving stones. Its eyes are white with Poseidon's madness.)
Stand before me. Every shade I have judged stood where you stand.
(Something huge breathes in the dark of the Labyrinth, and the floor shakes.)
(It knows you. The seventh labour; it has not forgotten the rope.)
The ground heaves under unseen giant blows!
Thor and his companions came to a castle so high they had to bend their heads back to see over it; inside, on two benches, sat a great many people, most of them huge.
Pale shapes of Utgarda-Loki's glamour, that burst like mist at a blow. When Thor turned to strike the king, the castle itself had vanished.
A copy of the giant king, made of nothing but glamour. While his copies stand, the king himself is hard to strike.

Utgarda-Loki's man in the eating contest. Loki ate all the meat off the bones in his half of the trough; Logi ate the meat, the bones and the trough too. He was wildfire itself, which burns everything.

The young man who raced Thjálfi, the fastest of men, three times, and each time was so far ahead he could turn round to meet him. Utgarda-Loki later told Thor the truth: Hugi was his own thought, and nothing is as fast as thought.

The king of the giants of Utgard. He was the giant Skrýmir who led Thor through the forest; the drinking horn was joined to the sea, the cat was the World Serpent, the old woman Elli was old age itself. All of it was illusion, and when Thor turned to strike him, the king and his castle had vanished.
Útgarða-Loki raises illusions! Break them to reach him!
Meat, bones, trough... and now you.
Run, if you like. I'll be there before you.
Welcome to Utgard, little ones. Nothing here is what it seems.
Thor! Did you ever finish that horn? The sea is still lower for it.
The walls shake, and stones fall!
The soldiers of the usurper Vortigern, in mail shirts and conical helms, who held Britain for him while his tower fell and fell again.

A strange beast Arthur saw drinking at a well: a serpent's head, a leopard's body, a lion's haunches and a hart's feet, and from its belly came a noise like thirty couple of hounds questing. King Pellinore had hunted it for twelve months and never caught it.
The noise of thirty couple of hounds drives you back!

Arthur's sister, a great sorceress. Merlin told Arthur the scabbard of Excalibur was worth ten of the sword, for while he wore it he would lose no blood. Morgan stole it, and when she was pursued she threw it far into a lake.
The scabbard has fallen! Take it, and she will bleed!

The usurper king of the Britons. The tower he built on Snowdon fell down every night, until the boy Merlin showed him why. In the end Aurelius Ambrosius besieged him in another tower and burned it down around him.
(From its belly comes a noise like thirty couple of hounds questing.)
The scabbard is worth ten of the sword. And it is mine.
This time the tower will stand.
Defeat the War Drummer before his sixth drumbeat. A war-paint aura.
Every beat brings more. Silence the drum quickly.
Tear down the Warlord's banner three times, then defeat him. Adds the Torn Banner passive.
Where the banner falls, the warriors falter.
Defeat Minos without ever being condemned. A golden-sceptre aura.
He condemns those who keep away. Stand before him.
Defeat Asterion before his fourth flurry of rushes. Adds the Ariadne's Thread passive.
Theseus didn't wander the Labyrinth. He went straight to the heart of it.
Defeat Hugi before he leaps ahead of you ten times. A thought-silver aura.
Nothing outruns thought. Don't race him; stop him.
Break two sets of Útgarða-Loki's illusions, then defeat him. Adds the Drinking Horn passive.
The horn was joined to the sea. See what is really there.
Take Excalibur's scabbard from Morgan le Fay three times, then defeat her. Adds the Scabbard Strap passive.
The scabbard is worth ten of the sword. Win it back.
Bring Vortigern's tower down with Fire twice, then defeat him. A tower-flame aura.
Aurelius did not storm the tower. He burned it.
Smoke and cinders roll out of Hephaestus' forge!
In his forge Hephaestus made works that moved by themselves: tripods on golden wheels that rolled to the gods' gathering and back. On his island they walk.
Hephaestus' servants, made of gold in the likeness of living girls; they have understanding, speech and strength, and skill from the gods.
Two bulls with feet of bronze that breathed fire, Hephaestus' gift to King Aeëtes. Jason had to yoke them alone and plough a field with them; Medea's ointment kept the fire from burning him.
On either side of the door of Alcinous' palace stood dogs of gold and silver, which Hephaestus had made with cunning skill to guard the house, immortal and ageless all their days.

A man of bronze who guarded Crete, running round the island three times a day and hurling rocks at ships. One vein ran from his neck down to his ankle, stopped with a bronze nail; when the nail came out, his ichor ran out and he fell.
Talos glows red-hot! Keep back, then strike the nail!
Defeat The Gold and Silver Hounds
(Fire roars from two bronze mouths. The ground smokes under their feet.)
(Two hounds of gold and silver, immortal and ageless, rise from beside the door.)
Three times round the island every day. Nothing lands that I don't see.
Earth-shaker, your ships do not land here.
